claim: Protein O-mannosyltransferases (PMTs) represent a conserved family of multispanning endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins involved in glycosylation of S/T-rich protein substrates and unfolded proteins.
source: Protein O-mannosyltransferases (PMTs) represent a conserved family of multispanning endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins involved in glycosylation of S/T-rich protein substrates and unfolded proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of PMTs, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: PMTs work as dimers.
source: PMTs work as dimers and contain a luminal MIR domain with a β-trefoil fold, which is susceptive for missense mutations causing α-dystroglycanopathies in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: PMTs contain a luminal MIR domain with a β-trefoil fold.
source: PMTs work as dimers and contain a luminal MIR domain with a β-trefoil fold, which is susceptive for missense mutations causing α-dystroglycanopathies in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The MIR domain is susceptive for missense mutations causing α-dystroglycanopathies in humans.
source: PMTs work as dimers and contain a luminal MIR domain with a β-trefoil fold, which is susceptive for missense mutations causing α-dystroglycanopathies in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed in the context of human disease mutations.

claim: Pmt2-MIR and Pmt3-MIR domain structures were determined.
source: We determine Pmt2- and Pmt3-MIR domain structures and identify two conserved mannose-binding sites, which are consistent with general β-trefoil carbohydrate-binding sites (α, β), and also a unique PMT2-subfamily exposed FKR motif.
evidence: The manuscript presents X-ray crystallography data for these structures.

claim: Two conserved mannose-binding sites (α, β) were identified in PMT-MIR domains, consistent with general β-trefoil carbohydrate-binding sites.
source: We determine Pmt2- and Pmt3-MIR domain structures and identify two conserved mannose-binding sites, which are consistent with general β-trefoil carbohydrate-binding sites (α, β), and also a unique PMT2-subfamily exposed FKR motif.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and comparison with other β-trefoil structures.

claim: A unique PMT2-subfamily exposed FKR motif was identified.
source: We determine Pmt2- and Pmt3-MIR domain structures and identify two conserved mannose-binding sites, which are consistent with general β-trefoil carbohydrate-binding sites (α, β), and also a unique PMT2-subfamily exposed FKR motif.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis and sequence alignment.

claim: Conserved residues in site α influence enzyme processivity of the Pmt1-Pmt2 heterodimer in vivo.
source: We show that conserved residues in site α influence enzyme processivity of the Pmt1-Pmt2 heterodimer in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo mutational analysis and substrate glycosylation assays.

claim: PMTs catalyze the transfer of mannose from dolichol monophosphate-activated mannose (Dol-P-Man) to the hydroxyl group of serine and threonine residues of proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: Protein O-mannosyltransferases (PMTs) of the PMT family are multispanning membrane glycosyltransferases (GT family 39; http://www.cazy.org) of the GT-C fold (Albuquerque-Wendt et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2019) that catalyze the transfer of mannose from dolichol monophosphate-activated mannose (Dol-P-Man) to the hydroxyl group of serine and threonine residues of proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (reviewed in Neubert and Strahl, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PMT-based O-mannosylation is an evolutionarily conserved and vital process, key for cell wall integrity and protein quality control in fungi.
source: PMT-based O-mannosylation is an evolutionarily conserved and vital process, key for cell wall integrity and protein quality control in fungi (Arroyo et al., 2011; Gentzsch and Tanner, 1996; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: In humans, impairment of classic type of O-mannosylation leads to a series of neuromuscular disorders due to α-dystroglycan hypo-glycosylation, known as α−dystroglycanopathies.
source: In humans, impairment of this classic type of O-mannosylation leads to a series of neuromuscular disorders, due to α-dystroglycan hypo-glycosylation, known as α−dystroglycanopathies (reviewed in Endo, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: PMTs are divided into three subfamilies (PMT1, PMT2, and PMT4).
source: PMTs are divided into three subfamilies (PMT1, PMT2, and PMT4) (reviewed in Neubert and Strahl, 2016) and form functional dimers either within or across subfamilies (Akasaka-Manya et al., 2006; Girrbach and Strahl, 2003; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: PMTs form functional dimers either within or across subfamilies.
source: PMTs are divided into three subfamilies (PMT1, PMT2, and PMT4) (reviewed in Neubert and Strahl, 2016) and form functional dimers either within or across subfamilies (Akasaka-Manya et al., 2006; Girrbach and Strahl, 2003; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Mammals have only two PMT proteins, POMT1 and POMT2, working as a heterodimer.
source: Mammals have only two PMT proteins, POMT1 and POMT2, working as a heterodimer (Akasaka-Manya et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae has seven different PMT family members, six of which have confirmed enzymatic activity (Pmt1-Pmt6).
source: Conversely, Saccharomyces cerevisiae has seven different PMT family members, six of which have confirmed enzymatic activity (Pmt1-Pmt6) (Gentzsch and Tanner, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Pmt4 homodimers and Pmt1-Pmt2 heterodimers account for the major O-mannosylation activity on both soluble and membrane protein substrates.
source: Pmt4 homodimers and Pmt1-Pmt2 heterodimers account for the major O-mannosylation activity on both soluble and membrane protein substrates (Gentzsch and Tanner, 1997; Hutzler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The loss of function of Pmt1 or Pmt2 is compensated for by the formation of alternative heterodimers, such as Pmt1-Pmt3 and Pmt5-Pmt2.
source: The loss of function of Pmt1 or Pmt2 is compensated for by the formation of alternative heterodimers, such as Pmt1-Pmt3 and Pmt5-Pmt2, which further explains the redundancy of PMT proteins in S. cerevisiae (Girrbach and Strahl, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The majority of yeast proteins entering the secretory pathway are O-mannosylated by PMTs.
source: The majority of yeast proteins entering the secretory pathway are O-mannosylated (O-Man) by PMTs, including more than 90% of all cell wall proteins that usually carry numerous O-mannosyl glycans (Neubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: More than 90% of all cell wall proteins carry numerous O-mannosyl glycans.
source: The majority of yeast proteins entering the secretory pathway are O-mannosylated (O-Man) by PMTs, including more than 90% of all cell wall proteins that usually carry numerous O-mannosyl glycans (Neubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: O-Mannosylation of PMT bona fide substrates occurs mainly in S/T-rich protein segments.
source: O-Mannosylation of PMT bona fide substrates occurs mainly in S/T-rich protein segments (Larsen et al., 2017; Neubert et al., 2016), whereas in ER protein quality control (referred to as unfolded protein O-mannosylation; UPOM) PMTs also target isolated serines and threonines of un- or misfolded proteins (reviewed in Xu and Ng, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: In ER protein quality control (UPOM), PMTs target isolated serines and threonines of un- or misfolded proteins.
source: O-Mannosylation of PMT bona fide substrates occurs mainly in S/T-rich protein segments (Larsen et al., 2017; Neubert et al., 2016), whereas in ER protein quality control (referred to as unfolded protein O-mannosylation; UPOM) PMTs also target isolated serines and threonines of un- or misfolded proteins (reviewed in Xu and Ng, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Only Pmt1-Pmt2 is involved in UPOM.
source: Remarkably, only Pmt1-Pmt2 is involved in UPOM (Castells-Ballester et al., 2019; Xu and Ng, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of the Pmt1-Pmt2 heterodimer from S. cerevisiae became available recently.
source: Only recently cryo-EM structures of the Pmt1-Pmt2 heterodimer from S. cerevisiae became available (Bai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Each PMT subunit has 11 transmembrane helices (TMHs).
source: In these structures each subunit has 11 transmembrane helices (TMHs) and two large hydrophilic loops oriented towards the ER lumen (LL): loop LL1 between TMH1 and 2 harboring a catalytic DE motif (Lommel et al., 2011), and loop LL4 between TMH7 and 8, encompassing a so-called MIR domain, whose function remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryo-EM structures.

claim: PMT subunits have two large hydrophilic loops oriented towards the ER lumen (LL).
source: In these structures each subunit has 11 transmembrane helices (TMHs) and two large hydrophilic loops oriented towards the ER lumen (LL): loop LL1 between TMH1 and 2 harboring a catalytic DE motif (Lommel et al., 2011), and loop LL4 between TMH7 and 8, encompassing a so-called MIR domain, whose function remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Loop LL1 is between TMH1 and 2 and harbors a catalytic DE motif.
source: In these structures each subunit has 11 transmembrane helices (TMHs) and two large hydrophilic loops oriented towards the ER lumen (LL): loop LL1 between TMH1 and 2 harboring a catalytic DE motif (Lommel et al., 2011), and loop LL4 between TMH7 and 8, encompassing a so-called MIR domain, whose function remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Loop LL4 is between TMH7 and 8 and encompasses a MIR domain.
source: In these structures each subunit has 11 transmembrane helices (TMHs) and two large hydrophilic loops oriented towards the ER lumen (LL): loop LL1 between TMH1 and 2 harboring a catalytic DE motif (Lommel et al., 2011), and loop LL4 between TMH7 and 8, encompassing a so-called MIR domain, whose function remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryo-EM structures.

claim: MIR domains have been annotated originally from sequence homologies detected between mannosyltransferases, inositol triphosphate receptors (IP3Rs) and ryanodine receptors (RyRs).
source: MIR domains have been annotated originally from sequence homologies detected between mannosyltransferases, inositol triphosphate receptors (IP3Rs) and ryanodine receptors (RyRs) (Ponting, 2000), which do not have a conserved protein function (MacKrill, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: MIR domains have a β-trefoil fold consisting of six β-hairpins arranged within a pseudo-threefold symmetry.
source: MIR domains have a β-trefoil fold consisting of six β-hairpins arranged within a pseudo-threefold symmetry.
evidence: This is stated and demonstrated by the structural data.

claim: The β-trefoil fold was originally identified in interleukin-1β and fibroblast growth factors.
source: This fold was originally identified in interleukin-1β and fibroblast growth factors (Murzin et al., 1992) but it is also present in many carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZy [Lombard et al., 2014]), such as the UDP-GalNAc:polypeptide GalNAc-transferases (GalNAc-Ts) that are responsible for mucin-type protein O-glycosylation in animals (Gill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The β-trefoil fold is present in many carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZy), such as UDP-GalNAc:polypeptide GalNAc-transferases (GalNAc-Ts).
source: This fold was originally identified in interleukin-1β and fibroblast growth factors (Murzin et al., 1992) but it is also present in many carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZy [Lombard et al., 2014]), such as the UDP-GalNAc:polypeptide GalNAc-transferases (GalNAc-Ts) that are responsible for mucin-type protein O-glycosylation in animals (Gill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: GalNAc-Ts are responsible for mucin-type protein O-glycosylation in animals.
source: This fold was originally identified in interleukin-1β and fibroblast growth factors (Murzin et al., 1992) but it is also present in many carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZy [Lombard et al., 2014]), such as the UDP-GalNAc:polypeptide GalNAc-transferases (GalNAc-Ts) that are responsible for mucin-type protein O-glycosylation in animals (Gill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: According to the CAZy classification, the MIR domain β-trefoils would belong to the carbohydrate-binding module (CBM) fold family 2 (CBM families 13 and 42).
source: Although not assigned yet, according to the CAZy classification (http://www.cazy.org), the MIR domain β-trefoils would belong to the carbohydrate-binding module (CBM) fold family 2 (CBM families 13 and 42; Boraston et al., 2004; Fujimoto, 2013; Lombard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Canonical CBM family 13 members are multivalent sugar binders and contain binding sites on each lateral face of the triangular domain named α, β, and γ.
source: Canonical CBM family 13 members are multivalent sugar binders and contain binding sites on each lateral face of the triangular domain named α, β, and γ (Boraston et al., 2004; Fujimoto, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: MIR domains of PMT1 and PMT2 family members (Pmt1, Pmt5, and Pmt2, Pmt3) were expressed in Escherichia coli and purified.
source: The MIR domains of PMT1 and PMT2 family members (Pmt1, Pmt5, and Pmt2, Pmt3) were expressed in Escherichia coli and purified.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: MIR domains of the PMT1 family proved to be unstable when analyzed by nano differential scanning fluorimetry (nanoDSF) and failed to crystallize.
source: While MIR domains of the PMT1 family proved to be unstable when analyzed by nano differential scanning fluorimetry (nanoDSF, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and failed to crystallize, PMT2 family MIR domains were more thermostable and readily formed crystals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by nanoDSF data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PMT2 family MIR domains were more thermostable and readily formed crystals.
source: While MIR domains of the PMT1 family proved to be unstable when analyzed by nano differential scanning fluorimetry (nanoDSF, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and failed to crystallize, PMT2 family MIR domains were more thermostable and readily formed crystals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by crystallization data.

claim: X-ray structures were determined by molecular replacement using the MIR domain of the stromal-derived factor 2 (SDF2) from Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: X-ray structures were determined by molecular replacement using the MIR domain of the stromal-derived factor 2 (SDF2) from Arabidopsis thaliana previously solved in our laboratory (Radzimanowski et al., 2010; Schott et al., 2010; Figure 1B,C and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The high resolution of the Pmt2-MIR (1.6 Å) and Pmt3-MIR (1.9 Å) structures allowed for a detailed analysis of the respective structural properties and ligand interactions.
source: The high resolution of the Pmt2-MIR (1.6 Å) and Pmt3-MIR (1.9 Å) structures allowed for a detailed analysis of the respective structural properties and ligand interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The MIR domains of the PMT2 family reveal the canonical β-trefoil fold (12 β-strands in total).
source: The MIR domains of the PMT2 family reveal the canonical β-trefoil fold (12 β-strands in total, PFAM trefoil clan CL0066, Figure 1C; Murzin et al., 1992), comprising a six-stranded β-barrel and a triangular β-hairpin cap including a hairpin triplet.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Despite a marginal sequence homology of below 20%, the PMT-MIR domains are structurally highly similar to the MIR domains of the IP3R and RyR proteins (root mean square deviation (rmsd) of approx. 1.6 Å).
source: Despite a marginal sequence homology of below 20%, the PMT-MIR domains are structurally highly similar to the MIR domains of the IP3R and RyR proteins (root mean square deviation (rmsd) of approx. 1.6 Å) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MIR domains consist of three trefoil MIR-motif units (MIRm1-3).
source: MIR domains consist of three trefoil MIR-motif units (Bai et al., 2019; Schott et al., 2010), in the following denoted MIRm1-3 (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations and shown in Figure 1B,D.

claim: Each MIR-motif comprises two β-hairpins, one in the barrel and one in the cap, and an extended connection between the hairpins that completes the trefoil unit.
source: Each MIR-motif comprises two β-hairpins, one in the barrel and one in the cap, and an extended connection between the hairpins that completes the trefoil unit (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The hydrophobic core of the MIR domains involves one conserved tryptophan and leucine residue per MIR-motif that together constitute a central triad arrangement of the core at the barrel-cap interface.
source: The hydrophobic core of the MIR domains involves one conserved tryptophan and leucine residue per MIR-motif that together constitute a central triad arrangement of the core at the barrel-cap interface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: Pmt2- and Pmt3-MIR domains have high sequence and structural similarity (68% identity, rmsd of 0.7 Å for 194 Cα-atoms).
source: Given the high sequence and structural similarity between Pmt2- and Pmt3-MIR domains (68% identity, rmsd of 0.7 Å for 194 Cα-atoms), we focused further analysis on the Pmt2-MIR domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparison.

claim: On the protein surface two regions reveal high sequence conservation, denoted as sites α and β.
source: On the protein surface two regions reveal high sequence conservation (Figure 3A), in the following denoted as sites α and β (residue ranges see Figure 2) in accordance with general CBM terminology (Boraston et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sites α and β localize to pronounced surface cavities in the cap region featuring a pair of histidines at their bottom.
source: These sites localize to pronounced surface cavities in the cap region featuring a pair of histidines at their bottom.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: Both cavities (sites α and β) are rather negatively charged.
source: Both cavities are rather negatively charged (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The histidines are part of conserved LH(S/T)H fingerprints present in MIRm1 strand β2 and MIRm2 strand β6.
source: The histidines are part of conserved LH(S/T)H fingerprints present in MIRm1 strand β2 and MIRm2 strand β6 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: For Pmt2, H362 and H364 are fixed in a defined orientation by a complex hydrogen-bonding pattern within the strictly conserved site α in the interface between MIRm1 and MIRm3.
source: For Pmt2, H362 and H364 are fixed in a defined orientation by a complex hydrogen-bonding pattern within the strictly conserved site α in the interface between MIRm1 and MIRm3 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MIRm1 site α is completed by residues Y380, D384, N386, F504, and Q506 forming the wall of the cavity.
source: MIRm1 site α, which is directly adjacent to the conserved L361 of the core, is completed by residues Y380, D384, N386, F504, and Q506 forming the wall of the cavity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: The 384-DxNN sequence is the second prominent conserved motif and constitutes the sole short helix (η1) within MIRm1.
source: The 384-DxNN sequence (x, any residue) is the second prominent conserved motif and constitutes the sole short helix (η1) within MIRm1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: An almost identical arrangement is found for Pmt2-MIR site β in the MIRm1-MIRm2 interface.
source: An almost identical arrangement is found for Pmt2-MIR site β in the MIRm1-MIRm2 interface (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both cavities (sites α and β) are filled by ligands present in the crystallization solvent (glycerol in site α and sulfate in site β).
source: Both cavities are filled by ligands present in the crystallization solvent (glycerol in site α [also in Pmt3] and sulfate in site β).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on crystallographic data.

claim: Pmt2-MIR displays a pseudo-threefold symmetry typical for the β-trefoil fold classified as Type C CBMs.
source: Although Pmt2-MIR displays a pseudo-threefold symmetry typical for the β-trefoil fold classified as Type C CBMs (Boraston et al., 2004), the analogous site γ (the third binding site present in β-trefoils) is not present in MIRm3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The analogous site γ (the third binding site present in β-trefoils) is not present in MIRm3.
source: Although Pmt2-MIR displays a pseudo-threefold symmetry typical for the β-trefoil fold classified as Type C CBMs (Boraston et al., 2004), the analogous site γ (the third binding site present in β-trefoils) is not present in MIRm3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: MIRm3 differs the most in sequence, with mainly key-residues like L492 and W524 of the core being conserved.
source: Overall, MIRm3 differs the most in sequence, with mainly key-residues like L492 and W524 of the core being conserved (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: On the surface of the β11-β12 loop a two-residue insertion is present, which is specific to the PMT2 family (including Pmt2, Pmt3, and Pmt6) and human POMTs.
source: However, on the surface of the β11-β12 loop a two-residue insertion is present, which is specific to the PMT2 family (including Pmt2, Pmt3, and Pmt6) and human POMTs (Figures 2 and 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2 and 3E.

claim: This loop forms a surface exposed ligand-binding site in Pmt2-MIR, defined as PMT2 family-specific site δ.
source: This loop forms a surface exposed ligand-binding site in Pmt2-MIR, from now on defined as PMT2 family-specific site δ.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: Site δ consists of F516, K517, and R518, of which only the arginine is conserved in other PMT-families.
source: It consists of F516, K517, and R518, of which only the arginine is conserved in other PMT-families.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: The three residues (F516, K517, R518) form a trident that has picked another glycerol ligand from the solvent via hydrogen-bonding to the arginine side chain and to the backbone amides within site δ.
source: The three residues form a trident that has picked another glycerol ligand from the solvent via hydrogen-bonding to the arginine side chain and to the backbone amides within site δ (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: MIRm3 site δ displays a pronounced positive surface potential.
source: Overall, MIRm3 site δ displays a pronounced positive surface potential (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Adjacent to site δ, another three surface exposed residues are highly conserved (E461, R482, Y491; site δa).
source: Adjacent to site δ, another three surface exposed residues are highly conserved (E461, R482, Y491; site δa) (Figures 2 and 3A), forming a tight patch that might act in concert with site δ.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2 and 3A.

claim: Sites α to δ are not conserved in MIR domains of RyR and IP3R family members.
source: From superposition of Pmt2-MIR with MIR domains of RyR and IP3R family members (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), it is evident that sites α to δ are not conserved and the evolutionary correlation within the MIR family remains obscure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Three putative ligand-binding sites were identified in the Pmt2- and Pmt3-MIR domains.
source: Taken together, we identified three putative ligand-binding sites in the Pmt2- and Pmt3-MIR domains.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the structural analysis.

claim: Two MIR-motifs form almost identical surface cavities and are conserved in all PMT-MIRs.
source: Two MIR-motifs form almost identical surface cavities and are conserved in all PMT-MIRs, while the third site is specific for MIRm3 of the PMT2 family and is highly solvent exposed.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the structural analysis.

claim: The third site is specific for MIRm3 of the PMT2 family and is highly solvent exposed.
source: Two MIR-motifs form almost identical surface cavities and are conserved in all PMT-MIRs, while the third site is specific for MIRm3 of the PMT2 family and is highly solvent exposed.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the structural analysis.

claim: A structure-based homology search found a close structural homology of PMT-MIRs to many lectins with small-sugar-binding Type C CBMs.
source: Besides the relationship of the PMT-MIRs to SDF2 (Schott et al., 2010) and within the MIR family, we found a close structural homology to many lectins with small-sugar-binding Type C CBMs (Boraston et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Other structurally related carbohydrate-binding β-trefoils were found in xylanases (PDB ID: 1isv) or galactosidases (PDB ID: 1ups).
source: Other structurally related carbohydrate-binding β-trefoils were found in xylanases (PDB ID: 1isv) or galactosidases (PDB ID: 1ups), thus justifying the general β-trefoil classification as CBMs in the CAZy database (Lombard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: In all compared β-trefoil structures, carbohydrate binding almost exclusively occurs at the triangular cap region (the hairpin triplet) and not at the β-barrel.
source: In all compared β-trefoil structures, carbohydrate binding almost exclusively occurs at the triangular cap region (the hairpin triplet) and not at the β-barrel (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The binding modes to sites α and β are highly conserved.
source: Most importantly, the analysis shows that the binding modes to sites α and β are highly conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparison.

claim: A corresponding carbohydrate-binding γ site within the third trefoil (MIRm3) is not present in Pmt2-MIR and is generally not conserved within the PMT family members.
source: However, a corresponding carbohydrate-binding γ site within the third trefoil (MIRm3) is not present in Pmt2-MIR and is generally not conserved within the PMT family members (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ligands found in Pmt2-MIR sites α and β match the sugar moieties in the compared structures.
source: Ligands found in Pmt2-MIR sites α and β match the sugar moieties in the compared structures (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The general theme for CBM-carbohydrate interactions is the packing of a sugar ring against a solvent exposed aromatic residue, while the hydroxyl-groups are bonded to a polar residue at the bottom of the sugar-binding cavity.
source: The general theme, as typical for CBM-carbohydrate interactions (Boraston et al., 2004), is the packing of a sugar ring (glycerol in Pmt2-MIR) against a solvent exposed aromatic residue (Y380 in Pmt2-MIRm1), while the hydroxyl-groups are bonded to a polar residue at the bottom of the sugar-binding cavity (H362 in Pmt2-MIRm1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Structure-based homology demonstrates the feasibility of ligand binding in Pmt2-MIR to the general β-trefoil carbohydrate-binding sites α and β.
source: In summary, structure-based homology demonstrates the feasibility of ligand binding in Pmt2-MIR to the general β-trefoil carbohydrate-binding sites α and β, suggesting its interaction with the mannose moiety of donor or acceptor substrates.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on structural comparison.

claim: Pmt2-MIR may interact with the mannose moiety of donor or acceptor substrates.
source: In summary, structure-based homology demonstrates the feasibility of ligand binding in Pmt2-MIR to the general β-trefoil carbohydrate-binding sites α and β, suggesting its interaction with the mannose moiety of donor or acceptor substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on structural comparison.

claim: More than half (56%) of the backbone amide resonances of Pmt2-MIR could be assigned using 3D triple-resonance experiments in combination with selective 15N-labeling of amino acids.
source: By using 3D triple-resonance experiments in combination with selective 15N-labeling of amino acids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), more than half (56%) of the backbone amide resonances could be assigned to structurally map putative interactions with mannose and derivatives by NMR screening and titration experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) show weak, but specific binding of mannose and α-mannose-1-phosphate to Pmt2-MIR.
